newsitem.title: THAILAND: Cash becoming king as Thai contractors feel pinch.
newsitem.headline: Cash becoming king as Thai contractors feel pinch.

text.p: The Thai construction industry is facing a growing liquidity squeeze brought on by the country's economic woes and property sector slump, executives and analysts said on Tuesday.
Thailand faces a number of economic problems including slowing gross domestic product growth and a property glut that could take up to five years to absorb.

Slowing growth was likely to lower corporate earnings while high interest rates, among the highest in the region at a minimum of 12.75 percent, had curbed demand and placed a heavy financing burden on domestic borrowers, analysts said.

The deteriorating environment has already induced a number of corporate failures in Thailand. Medium-sized developer Somprasong Land defaulted on a $3.1 million Eurobond coupon in January, and analysts widely expect some highly geared developers to fail in coming months.

Property sector woes were filtering down to the construction sector where firms had increasing problems extending supplier credit and faced growing difficulties collecting payment for completed works from developers, executives said.

"At our level it hasn't been a problem up to yet but it could be a problem right now for smaller companies...for them the liquidity crunch is on," said a senior official at Ch Karnchang Plc, one the country's largest contractors.

"Some of our dealers are having some problems collecting payment from their clients...Those clients are probably going to be smaller contractors doing private work and I think their problems stem from the property sector," said an executive at Jalaprathan Cement Plc

Major building materials suppliers were dealing with a growing number of customers on a cash payment basis as bank guarantees became harder to obtain, and payment problems among clients became more commonplace, executives said.

"Our normal credit terms are 60 days with a bank guarantee. For clients without a guarantee we ask for cash with orders, and from our dealers cash on delivery," said a senior member of the finance department at Thailand's largest conglomerate, Siam Cement Plc
"The amount of cash with order business has increased and we have had a lot more cheques being returned this year ... many from (building) contractors but also from some dealers," the executive said.

Smaller contractors were likely to be squeezed more still as private developers put an increasing number of existing and planned building projects on hold until property market conditions improved, executives said.

Larger constructors, more heavily reliant on government work, were largely unaffected despite fears the government might have to further cut its infrastructure budget to match declining tax revenues from firms reporting lower-than-expected profits, analysts said.

A 40 billion baht ($1.54 billion) cut in planned infrastructure spending announced earlier this year prompted many large construction firms to predict that they may compete on smaller government works.
That could push medium-sized contractors to look for larger private sector contracts at a time when order books are looking thinner.
"The private work is very quiet and the order books across the industry now must be fairly grim," said the CH Karnchang executive.
